title: Load Balancer — what it does (distributes traffic), types (L4 vs L7), algorithms (round-robin, least connections, IP hash), health checks, and when to use (every production system needs one).

s1_definition.profdef: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across a pool of backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and provide fault tolerance. Layer 4 load balancers route by transport-level information such as IP and port, while Layer 7 load balancers route by application-level information such as HTTP path or headers. They apply a distribution algorithm, run health checks to route only to healthy backends, and are a mandatory component of any production system that runs more than one server.
s1_definition.analogy: When customers crowd into National Bank of India, a floor manager stands at the entrance and directs each person to an open teller so no single teller is overwhelmed while others sit idle. If a teller goes on break, the manager stops sending people there. The load balancer is that floor manager for servers: it spreads requests evenly, skips any server that is down, and makes the whole branch feel fast and reliable even when some tellers are unavailable.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spread traffic across healthy servers using an algorithm, route by connection (L4) or by request content (L7), and never send traffic to a server that failed its health check.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across a pool of backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and provide fault tolerance. Layer 4 load balancers route by transport-level information such as IP and port, while Layer 7 load balancers route by application-level information such as HTTP path or headers. They apply a distribution algorithm, run health checks to route only to healthy backends, and are a mandatory component of any production system that runs more than one server.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When customers crowd into National Bank of India, a floor manager stands at the entrance and directs each person to an open teller so no single teller is overwhelmed while others sit idle. If a teller goes on break, the manager stops sending people there. The load balancer is that floor manager for servers: it spreads requests evenly, skips any server that is down, and makes the whole branch feel fast and reliable even when some tellers are unavailable.

**One line to remember:** Spread traffic across healthy servers using an algorithm, route by connection (L4) or by request content (L7), and never send traffic to a server that failed its health check.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs its transfer API on several servers, and on salary day one server was getting most of the traffic while others sat idle, so it slowed down and some transfers timed out. The real problem is uneven distribution. This is exactly what a load balancing algorithm fixes.

Problem 2 — one server crashed, but requests kept being sent to it, so customers saw errors. The real problem is routing to dead servers. This is exactly what health checks prevent.

Problem 3 — statement downloads are heavy and transfers are light, and the bank wants them handled by different server pools. The real problem is content-based routing. This is exactly what Layer 7 routing provides.

We build a runnable load balancer core: a `BackendPool` of servers with health status and connection counts, a `LoadBalancer` supporting round-robin, least-connections, and IP-hash algorithms plus L7 path routing, and a `HealthChecker`. The demo distributes requests across healthy servers, marks one unhealthy and shows it skipped, and routes by path.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three transfer servers, a series of requests, a health event marking one server down, connection counts, a client IP, and a statement path.

Step 1: Five round-robin requests cycle through the healthy servers in order, returning transfer-1, transfer-2, transfer-3, then wrapping around, which spreads load evenly.

Step 2: The health checker marks transfer-2 unhealthy. The next requests only cycle between transfer-1 and transfer-3, because the healthy list no longer includes transfer-2, so no request reaches the dead server.

Step 3: Connection counts are set, with transfer-1 busy at ten and transfer-3 light at two. Least-connections picks transfer-3 because it has the fewest active connections, which balances load by actual work rather than raw count.

Step 4: IP hash for a client maps consistently to one healthy server, giving that client stickiness. The L7 router inspects the statement path and returns the statement pool. The data that changed is which server each request is routed to, driven by health status and algorithm.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client requests
    │
    ▼
  LoadBalancer (pool of healthy backends)
    │
    ├─ round-robin → cycle 1,2,3,1,2...
    ├─ least-conns → server with fewest active
    ├─ ip-hash → stable server per client IP
    └─ L7 path → /api/transfers→transfer-pool, /api/statements→statement-pool
    │
    │ HealthChecker probes GET /health
    │  transfer-2 fails → removed from healthy()
    ▼
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │transfer-1│  │transfer-2│  │transfer-3│
  │ healthy  │  │ DOWN   │  │ healthy  │
  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘
       (traffic skips the unhealthy backend)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Load Balancer ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy: pluggable algorithm (RR/least-conn/IP-hash)    │
  │  Health check: remove failed backends from rotation       │
  │  L7 routing: content-based dispatch                       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Pool holds backends, LB routes, Checker probes        │
  │  O: new algorithm = new method, pool unchanged            │
  │  D: LB depends on BackendPool abstraction                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐
  │     LoadBalancer     │─────▶│      BackendPool     │
  │ - pool, counter      │ uses │ + add/get/healthy    │
  │ + roundRobin         │      └──────────┬───────────┘
  │ + leastConnections   │                 │ contains *
  │ + ipHash / routeL7   │                 ▼
  └──────────────────────┘      ┌──────────────────────┐
  ┌──────────────────────┐      │       Backend        │
  │    HealthChecker     │─────▶│ - healthy, activeConns│
  │ + markHealthy/Unhealthy│    │ + is/setHealthy      │
  └──────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Backend ─────────────────────────────────

  [HEALTHY] ──health check fails──→ [UNHEALTHY] (out of rotation)
      ▲                                  │
      └────── health check recovers ─────┘

  ── Call Chain (routing) ───────────────────────────────────

  1. lb.roundRobin()
  2.   → pool.healthy() → [transfer-1, transfer-3]
  3.   → index = counter++ % size
  4.   → return server id
  (health checker concurrently removes failed backends)

  Contract for roundRobin():
    Pre:  at least one healthy backend
    Post: returns next healthy backend in rotation
    Never returns an unhealthy backend
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across a pool of backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and survive failures, and it is a mandatory component of any production system that runs more than one server. Without it you can only scale up a single machine, which has a hard ceiling and is a single point of failure. With it you scale out across many servers and tolerate losing any one of them.

I always distinguish Layer 4 from Layer 7. A Layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer and forwards based on IP and port without reading the request, which is extremely fast and protocol-agnostic. A Layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request and can route by URL path, cookies, or headers, which at National Bank of India let me send heavy statement downloads to one server pool and light transfer requests to another. In practice a production stack often uses both: a fast Layer 4 balancer in front for TLS and raw throughput, and a Layer 7 balancer behind it for content-based routing.

The distribution algorithm decides which backend gets the next request. Round-robin cycles through servers and is fair when they are equal; least-connections sends to the least busy server and is better when request durations vary; IP hash maps each client consistently to one server for stickiness. The algorithm fixed a real problem for us on salary day, when one server was getting most of the transfer traffic while others sat idle, and switching to least-connections evened out the load and stopped the timeouts.

The piece that makes a load balancer trustworthy is health checks. The balancer periodically probes each backend's health endpoint and removes any server that fails from rotation until it recovers, so clients never hit a dead server, which is exactly what stopped customers seeing errors after one of our servers crashed. The senior nuance I always add is to keep the servers stateless and store session data in a shared cache rather than relying on sticky sessions, because stickiness hurts even distribution and complicates failover. And because the balancer itself must not become a new single point of failure, it is deployed as a highly available pair. That combination of smart distribution, content-aware routing, health checking, and high availability is why every serious production system has a load balancer at its front door.
